claim: DTT causes stress in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by disrupting its oxidative protein folding environment.
source: The redox reagent dithiothreitol (DTT) causes stress in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by disrupting its oxidative protein folding environment, which results in the accumulation and misfolding of the newly synthesized proteins.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about DTT's mechanism of action in the ER.

claim: DTT disruption of the ER oxidative environment results in the accumulation and misfolding of newly synthesized proteins.
source: The redox reagent dithiothreitol (DTT) causes stress in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by disrupting its oxidative protein folding environment, which results in the accumulation and misfolding of the newly synthesized proteins.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about ER stress mechanisms.

claim: DTT toxicity is modulated by the bacterial diet in C. elegans.
source: Using the nematode model Caenorhabditis elegans, here we show that DTT toxicity is modulated by the bacterial diet.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential development of C. elegans on different bacterial diets in the presence of DTT.

claim: Dietary vitamin B12 alleviates DTT toxicity in a methionine synthase-dependent manner.
source: Specifically, the dietary component vitamin B12 alleviates DTT toxicity in a methionine synthase-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of DTT toxicity by vitamin B12 supplementation and the requirement of methionine synthase (METR-1) for this rescue.

claim: Loss-of-function of R08E5.3, an S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferase, confers DTT resistance.
source: Using a forward genetic screen, we discover that loss-of-function of R08E5.3, an S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferase, confers DTT resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a forward genetic screen that identified 12 loss-of-function alleles of R08E5.3 (rips-1) that confer DTT resistance.

claim: DTT upregulates R08E5.3 expression.
source: DTT upregulates R08E5.3 expression and modulates the activity of the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and GFP reporter strain data showing increased rips-1 expression upon DTT exposure.

claim: DTT modulates the activity of the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
source: DTT upregulates R08E5.3 expression and modulates the activity of the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic and biochemical data showing that DTT affects SAM levels and that vitamin B12 and methionine supplementation rescue DTT toxicity.

claim: DTT toxicity is a result of the depletion of SAM.
source: Employing genetic and biochemical studies, we establish that DTT toxicity is a result of the depletion of SAM.
evidence: This claim is supported by SAM quantification data showing reduced SAM levels upon DTT exposure, and rescue experiments with methionine and choline supplementation.

claim: A functional IRE-1/XBP-1 unfolded protein response pathway is required to counteract toxicity at high, but not low, DTT concentrations.
source: Finally, we show that a functional IRE-1/XBP-1 unfolded protein response pathway is required to counteract toxicity at high, but not low, DTT concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that ire-1 and xbp-1 mutants can be rescued by vitamin B12 at 5 mM DTT but not at 10 mM DTT.

claim: C. elegans was at the L1 or L2 stage at 5 mM and higher DTT concentrations at 72 hr of hatching on E. coli OP50 diet.
source: In the presence of Escherichia coli OP50 diet, C. elegans was at the L1 or L2 stage at 5 mM and higher DTT concentrations at 72 hr of hatching, while the control animals without DTT had developed to adulthood at the same time (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Control C. elegans animals without DTT developed to adulthood at 72 hr of hatching on E. coli OP50 diet.
source: In the presence of Escherichia coli OP50 diet, C. elegans was at the L1 or L2 stage at 5 mM and higher DTT concentrations at 72 hr of hatching, while the control animals without DTT had developed to adulthood at the same time (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: C. elegans developed much better on DTT in the presence of E. coli HT115 diet than E. coli OP50 diet.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that C. elegans developed much better on DTT in the presence of E. coli HT115 diet than E. coli OP50 diet (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data comparing OP50 and HT115 diets shown in Figures 1A-C.

claim: Some bacterial components might be able to modulate DTT toxicity.
source: These results suggested that some bacterial components might be able to modulate DTT toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different bacterial diets result in different levels of DTT toxicity.

claim: C. elegans showed no developmental defects on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets in the presence of 10 mM DTT.
source: Interestingly, C. elegans showed no developmental defects on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets in the presence of 10 mM DTT (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: C. elegans developed much better on S. enterica and S. marcescens diets compared to the E. coli OP50 diet at lower DTT concentrations.
source: Similarly, C. elegans developed much better on S. enterica and S. marcescens diets compared to the E. coli OP50 diet at lower DTT concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Bacterial diet has a major effect on DTT toxicity.
source: These results showed that bacterial diet has a major effect on DTT toxicity, and likely some bacterial diet component(s) modulated DTT toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing differential DTT toxicity on different bacterial diets.

claim: Some bacterial diet component(s) likely modulated DTT toxicity.
source: These results showed that bacterial diet has a major effect on DTT toxicity, and likely some bacterial diet component(s) modulated DTT toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different bacterial diets result in different levels of DTT toxicity.

claim: Relative to the E. coli OP50 diet, a C. aquatica DA1877 diet accelerates C. elegans development primarily because it contains higher levels of vitamin B12.
source: Previous studies have shown that relative to the E. coli OP50 diet, a C. aquatica DA1877 diet accelerates C. elegans development primarily because it contains higher levels of vitamin B12 (Watson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claim: E. coli HT115 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets are known to have higher amounts of vitamin B12 than the E. coli OP50 diet.
source: Similarly, E. coli HT115 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets are known to have higher amounts of vitamin B12 than the E. coli OP50 diet (Revtovich et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Revtovich et al., 2019 and Watson et al., 2014.

claim: The amount of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans can be reliably determined by a dietary sensor strain expressing GFP under the promoter of acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (acdh-1) gene.
source: The amount of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans can be reliably determined by a dietary sensor strain expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP) under the promoter of acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (acdh-1) gene (Watson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claim: Low levels of vitamin B12 result in the accumulation of the short-chain fatty acid propionate, which leads to transcriptional activation of acdh-1.
source: Low levels of vitamin B12 result in the accumulation of the short-chain fatty acid propionate, which leads to transcriptional activation of acdh-1 (Watson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claim: GFP levels in the acdh-1p::GFP animals indirectly report the levels of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans.
source: Thus, the GFP levels in the acdh-1p::GFP animals indirectly report the levels of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism described by Watson et al., 2014.

claim: When animals experience low levels of vitamin B12, acdh-1p::GFP is strongly induced.
source: When the animals experience low levels of vitamin B12, acdh-1p::GFP is strongly induced, and the level of GFP expression reduces as the animals obtain increasing levels of vitamin B12.
evidence: This is based on the mechanism described by Watson et al., 2014.

claim: The level of GFP expression in acdh-1p::GFP animals reduces as the animals obtain increasing levels of vitamin B12.
source: When the animals experience low levels of vitamin B12, acdh-1p::GFP is strongly induced, and the level of GFP expression reduces as the animals obtain increasing levels of vitamin B12.
evidence: This is based on the mechanism described by Watson et al., 2014.

claim: Animals show very bright GFP expression on the E. coli OP50 diet.
source: As shown in Figure 1F and reported previously (Watson et al., 2014), the animals show very bright GFP expression on the E. coli OP50 diet, while the GFP levels were diminished on E. coli HT115, S. enterica, and S. marcescens diets.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1F and citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claim: GFP levels in acdh-1p::GFP animals were diminished on E. coli HT115, S. enterica, and S. marcescens diets.
source: As shown in Figure 1F and reported previously (Watson et al., 2014), the animals show very bright GFP expression on the E. coli OP50 diet, while the GFP levels were diminished on E. coli HT115, S. enterica, and S. marcescens diets.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Animals showed no GFP expression on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets.
source: On the other hand, the animals showed no GFP expression on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The levels of GFP expression in acdh-1p::GFP animals on different bacterial diets correlated perfectly with the developmental defects on these bacterial diets in the presence of DTT.
source: The levels of GFP expression in acdh-1p::GFP animals on different bacterial diets correlated perfectly with the developmental defects on these bacterial diets in the presence of DTT (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claim: Vitamin B12 could be the microbial component that alleviates DTT toxicity in C. elegans.
source: The correlation between the GFP levels in acdh-1p::GFP animals and the developmental defects of animals in the presence of DTT on different bacterial diets suggested that vitamin B12 could be the microbial component that alleviates DTT toxicity in C. elegans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between vitamin B12 levels (as reported by acdh-1p::GFP) and DTT toxicity.

claim: Wild-type N2 animals developed to adulthood on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT supplemented with 50 nM vitamin B12.
source: The wild-type N2 animals had improved development when 10 mM DTT containing E. coli OP50 diet was supplemented with varying concentrations of methionine (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: More than 95% of the animals developed to adulthood after 48 hr of incubation post vitamin B12 supplementation.
source: After 48 hr of incubation post vitamin B12 supplementation, more than 95% of the animals developed to adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Control animals on E. coli OP50 plates containing 10 mM DTT, but without vitamin B12 supplementation, were still at the L1–L2 stages after 120 hr of hatching.
source: On the other hand, the control animals on E. coli OP50 plates containing 10 mM DTT, but without vitamin B12 supplementation, were still at the L1–L2 stages after 120 hr of hatching.
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Vitamin B12 is sufficient to alleviate and revert the toxic effects of DTT.
source: Taken together, these studies showed that vitamin B12 is sufficient to alleviate and revert the toxic effects of DTT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing rescue of DTT toxicity by vitamin B12 supplementation.

claim: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans).
source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about vitamin B12 function.

claim: MMCM-1 converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway.
source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MMCM-1 function.

claim: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans).
source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about vitamin B12 function.

claim: METR-1 converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about METR-1 function.

claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation rescued the toxic effects of DTT in mmcm-1(ok1637) animals.
source: While vitamin B12 supplementation rescued the toxic effects of DTT in mmcm-1(ok1637) animals, it failed to do so in metr-1(ok521) animals (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation failed to rescue the toxic effects of DTT in metr-1(ok521) animals.
source: While vitamin B12 supplementation rescued the toxic effects of DTT in mmcm-1(ok1637) animals, it failed to do so in metr-1(ok521) animals (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: metr-1(ok521) animals were at the L1 stage on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT regardless of vitamin B12 supplementation.
source: The metr-1(ok521) animals were at the L1 stage on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT regardless of vitamin B12 supplementation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mmcm-1(ok1637) animals did not show any significant development retardation effects when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT.
source: Further, mmcm-1(ok1637) animals did not show any significant development retardation effects when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: metr-1(ok521) animals failed to develop when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT.
source: On the other hand, metr-1(ok521) animals failed to develop when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Vitamin B12 could alleviate DTT toxicity via the methionine synthase enzyme.
source: Taken together, these studies showed that vitamin B12 could alleviate DTT toxicity via the methionine synthase enzyme.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that vitamin B12 rescue requires functional METR-1 but not MMCM-1.

claim: Approximately 50,000 ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized haploid genomes were screened in the forward genetic screen.
source: From a screen of approximately 50,000 ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized haploid genomes, 12 mutants were isolated that exhibited DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: 12 mutants were isolated that exhibited DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT.
source: From a screen of approximately 50,000 ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized haploid genomes, 12 mutants were isolated that exhibited DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: All of the mutants had linkage to chromosome V.
source: All of the mutants had linkage to chromosome V.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: All of the mutants had a mutation in the gene R08E5.3.
source: Analysis of the protein-coding genes carrying mutations in the linked regions of each mutant revealed that all of the mutants had a mutation in the gene R08E5.3 (Figure 3A, B), which was recently named as rips-1 (Rhy-1-Interacting Protein in Sulfide response) (personal communication with Wormbase).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: R08E5.3 was recently named as rips-1 (Rhy-1-Interacting Protein in Sulfide response).
source: Analysis of the protein-coding genes carrying mutations in the linked regions of each mutant revealed that all of the mutants had a mutation in the gene R08E5.3 (Figure 3A, B), which was recently named as rips-1 (Rhy-1-Interacting Protein in Sulfide response) (personal communication with Wormbase).
evidence: This is information obtained from personal communication with Wormbase.

claim: rips-1 is predicted to encode a protein with a SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain.
source: rips-1 is predicted to encode a protein with a SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction of protein domain structure.

claim: SAM-dependent methyltransferases catalyze diverse methylation reactions where a methyl group is transferred to the substrate from SAM.
source: SAM-dependent methyltransferases catalyze diverse methylation reactions where a methyl group is transferred to the substrate from SAM, resulting in the conversion of SAM to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SAM-dependent methyltransferases.

claim: SAM-dependent methyltransferases result in the conversion of SAM to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
source: SAM-dependent methyltransferases catalyze diverse methylation reactions where a methyl group is transferred to the substrate from SAM, resulting in the conversion of SAM to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SAM-dependent methyltransferases.

claim: rips-1(gk231506) animals showed DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT.
source: rips-1(gk231506) animals showed DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Three of the isolated alleles of rips-1 (jsn4, jsn11, and jsn12) had premature stop codon mutations.
source: Three of the isolated alleles of rips-1, jsn4, jsn11, and jsn12 had premature stop codon mutations and one allele (jsn8) had a splice acceptor mutation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: One allele of rips-1 (jsn8) had a splice acceptor mutation.
source: Three of the isolated alleles of rips-1, jsn4, jsn11, and jsn12 had premature stop codon mutations and one allele (jsn8) had a splice acceptor mutation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All of the rips-1 mutations (jsn4, jsn8, jsn11, and jsn12) are expected to result in a loss-of-function of the gene.
source: All of these mutations are expected to result in a loss-of-function of the gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the mutations (premature stop codons and splice acceptor mutation).

claim: The DTT-resistant phenotype of rips-1(jsn11) animals was completely rescued by expressing rips-1 under its own promoter.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, the DTT-resistant phenotype of rips-1(jsn11) animals was completely rescued in these animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: rips-1 is expressed in the intestine.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, rips-1 is expressed in the intestine.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data of rips-1p::GFP animals shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In the fungus Aspergillus niger, DTT is known to highly upregulate two SAM-dependent methyltransferases.
source: In the fungus Aspergillus niger, DTT is known to highly upregulate two SAM-dependent methyltransferases (MacKenzie et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to MacKenzie et al., 2005.

claim: rips-1 shares high sequence similarity with three other SAM-dependent methyltransferases in C. elegans: R08E5.1, R08F11.4, and K12D9.1.
source: rips-1 shares high sequence similarity with three other SAM-dependent methyltransferases in C. elegans, R08E5.1 (BLAST e value: 1e−168), R08F11.4 (BLAST e value: 1e−166), and K12D9.1 (BLAST e value: 2e−152).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLAST sequence similarity analysis.

claim: DTT resulted in significant upregulation of the transcript levels of rips-1, R08E5.1, and R08F11.4.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis showed that DTT resulted in significant upregulation of the transcript levels of rips-1, R08E5.1, and R08F11.4 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The enhanced expression of rips-1 was confirmed in a reporter strain expressing GFP under the promoter of rips-1.
source: The enhanced expression of rips-1 was confirmed in a reporter strain expressing GFP under the promoter of rips-1 (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: Knockdown of rips-1 in the N2 animals resulted in a drastic improvement in their development in the presence of DTT.
source: As expected, knockdown of rips-1 in the N2 animals resulted in a drastic improvement in their development in the presence of DTT (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: Knockdown of R08E5.1 resulted in a phenotype similar to rips-1 knockdown.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of R08E5.1 resulted in a phenotype similar to rips-1 knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: Knockdown of R08F11.4 and K12D9.1 improved the development in the presence of DTT only marginally.
source: On the other hand, knockdown of R08F11.4 and K12D9.1 improved the development in the presence of DTT only marginally (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: The rips-1-related methyltransferases might be required for DTT toxicity.
source: These results suggest that the rips-1-related methyltransferases might also be required for DTT toxicity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the RNAi knockdown results.

claim: The knockdown of rips-1-related methyltransferases might result in the knockdown of rips-1 by cross RNAi.
source: It is also possible that the knockdown of these methyltransferases results in the knockdown of rips-1 by cross RNAi.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation for the RNAi results.

claim: The level of sequence similarity between rips-1 and R08E5.1 (78% identical) indicates that these genes would undergo complete cross RNAi.
source: The level of sequence similarity between rips-1 and R08E5.1 (78 % identical) indicates that these genes would undergo complete cross RNAi (Rual et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rual et al., 2007 regarding cross RNAi thresholds.

claim: The rips-1-related methyltransferases likely have only minor roles in DTT toxicity.
source: Because we did not recover mutants of any of the rips-1-related methyltransferases in our genetic screen in contrast to the 12 alleles of rips-1, the rips-1-related methyltransferases likely have only minor roles in DTT toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results of the genetic screen.

claim: Animals overexpressing rips-1 exhibited enhanced sensitivity to DTT toxicity.
source: Animals overexpressing rips-1 exhibited enhanced sensitivity to DTT toxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and 3D.

claim: By increasing the expression of rips-1, DTT modulates the methionine–homocysteine cycle resulting in toxic effects that can be reversed by supplementation of vitamin B12.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that by increasing the expression of rips-1, DTT modulates the methionine–homocysteine cycle resulting in toxic effects that can be reversed by supplementation of vitamin B12 (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing DTT upregulation of rips-1 and rescue by vitamin B12.

claim: Modulation of the methionine–homocysteine cycle or low dietary vitamin B12 are known to upregulate the mitochondrial UPR.
source: Modulation of the methionine–homocysteine cycle or low dietary vitamin B12 are known to upregulate the mitochondrial UPR (Amin et al., 2020; Wei and Ruvkun, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2020 and Wei and Ruvkun, 2020.

claim: Animals exposed to 10 mM DTT had upregulation of the mitochondrial UPR compared to control animals.
source: Compared to the control animals, animals exposed to 10 mM DTT had upregulation of the mitochondrial UPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by hsp-6p::GFP fluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claim: Supplementation of vitamin B12 rescued the upregulation of mitochondrial UPR by DTT.
source: Supplementation of vitamin B12 rescued the upregulation of mitochondrial UPR by DTT, indicating that DTT-induced mitochondrial UPR via the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by hsp-6p::GFP fluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claim: DTT-induced mitochondrial UPR via the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
source: Supplementation of vitamin B12 rescued the upregulation of mitochondrial UPR by DTT, indicating that DTT-induced mitochondrial UPR via the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of mitochondrial UPR by vitamin B12.

claim: rips-1(jsn11) animals exhibited resistance to β-ME toxicity.
source: Interestingly, rips-1(jsn11) animals exhibited resistance to β-ME toxicity, but not NAC toxicity (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: rips-1(jsn11) animals did not exhibit resistance to NAC toxicity.
source: Interestingly, rips-1(jsn11) animals exhibited resistance to β-ME toxicity, but not NAC toxicity (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: NAC exposure did not affect the expression of rips-1p::GFP.
source: While NAC exposure did not affect the expression of rips-1p::GFP, β-ME resulted in its dramatic upregulation (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: β-ME resulted in dramatic upregulation of rips-1p::GFP expression.
source: While NAC exposure did not affect the expression of rips-1p::GFP, β-ME resulted in its dramatic upregulation (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation alleviated β-ME toxicity.
source: Vitamin B12 supplementation alleviated β-ME, but not NAC, toxicity (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation did not alleviate NAC toxicity.
source: Vitamin B12 supplementation alleviated β-ME, but not NAC, toxicity (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: β-ME shares the toxicity mechanism with DTT.
source: These results suggested that β-ME shares the toxicity mechanism with DTT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar effects of β-ME and DTT on rips-1 expression and rescue by vitamin B12.

claim: NAC causes toxicity by a mechanism different from DTT.
source: On the other hand, NAC causes toxicity by a mechanism different from DTT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the different effects of NAC compared to DTT on rips-1 expression and lack of rescue by vitamin B12.

claim: The wild-type N2 animals had improved development when 10 mM DTT containing E. coli OP50 diet was supplemented with varying concentrations of methionine.
source: The wild-type N2 animals had improved development when 10 mM DTT containing E. coli OP50 diet was supplemented with varying concentrations of methionine (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Methionine supplementation alleviated DTT toxicity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Methionine supplementation alleviated DTT toxicity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: metr-1(ok521) animals that failed to develop upon vitamin B12 supplementation in the presence of DTT developed upon supplementation of methionine.
source: We observed that metr-1(ok521) animals that failed to develop upon vitamin B12 supplementation in the presence of DTT (Figure 2C, D), developed upon supplementation of methionine (Figure 5A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 5A and 5C.

claim: Depletion of methionine and/or SAM is the primary cause of DTT toxicity.
source: These results suggested that depletion of methionine and/or SAM is the primary cause of DTT toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue of DTT toxicity by methionine supplementation.
